name: Persistence via scheduled task
summary: An intruder stages a script in ProgramData, registers a scheduled task to run it at every logon, and the task fires. All artifacts are real and visible to the EDR, but benign: the script only appends a line to a log file.
objectives: Find the staged script, the scheduled task, and the task-launched PowerShell in the EDR.
Reconstruct the timeline: who wrote the script, who registered the task, what it ran.
Agree how this would be detected, contained, and eradicated in production.

parameters.name: ArtifactFolder
parameters.description: Folder under %ProgramData% where the script and its log are written. Each session gets its own subfolder.

parameters.name: ScriptName
parameters.description: File name of the benign stand-in script.

parameters.name: TaskName
parameters.description: Name of the scheduled task (registered in the root Task Scheduler folder).

steps.title: Stage a script in ProgramData
facilitatorNotes: Setting: the intruder already has a foothold as a user and drops a PowerShell script into a world-writable folder.
Analysts: find the new .ps1 under C:\ProgramData. What wrote it, when, and as which user?
Discuss: would anything alert on this today? Is script-write telemetry retained long enough?

steps.title: Register a scheduled task that runs the script at logon
facilitatorNotes: Setting: the intruder registers a task with an innocent-looking name so the script survives reboots.
Analysts: find the task registration. What is its trigger and exact command line?
Hint if stuck: look for task registration events, or the task XML under C:\Windows\System32\Tasks.
Discuss: how would we tell this apart from legitimate updater tasks?

steps.title: The task fires and runs the script
facilitatorNotes: Setting: the user logs on; the task fires and runs the script hidden.
Analysts: find powershell.exe launched by the Task Scheduler (parent svchost.exe) and what it wrote.
Discuss: containment and eradication steps. Who owns them, and how fast could we do it?
